Individuals who completed the survey were prompted to voluntarily enter their email for participation in a gift card raffle; to maintain anonymity, survey results were not connected with the email entered for raffle participation.

Statistical analyses were performed with GraphPad Prism Software 7.0c (La Jolla, CA). Categorical variables were assessed with the Pearson chi-squared test and Fisher exact t test. Nonparametric continuous variables were compared with a Wilcoxon ranksum test. Probability values <0.05 were considered significant. Given the small sample size of transgender/genderqueer (n ¼ 1), this individual was excluded from the statistical analysis because of power and to preserve anonymity. However, responses were noted where appropriate, particularly regarding free-text response.

RESULTS Approximately 720 medical students were surveyed and 261 completed the questionnaire (36.3% response rate). Demographics are reported in Table 1. Respondents were 58.6% women, 41% men, and 0.4% transgender.

Pursuing the Career

Of 260 individuals who reported career intent, 24.2% of students were pursuing a career in surgery, 53.5% were not, and 22.3% remained undecided. Responses for those pursuing a career in surgery encompassed individuals interested in all surgical fields and were not restricted to general surgery. Of those pursuing a career in surgery, respondents indicated their top 3 fields of surgical interest, which were in order of popularity general surgery (30.2%), orthopedic surgery (27.0%), plastic surgery (19.0%), thoracic surgery (17.5%), gynecological surgery (15.9%), otolaryngology (14.3%), urology (12.7%), pediatric surgery (11.1%), cardiac surgery (9.5%), ophthalmology (7.9%), and neurosurgery (7.9%). Overall, there was no significant difference between men and women in intention to pursue surgery (27% of men, 22% of women; P ¼ 0.38). However, more women were undecided about pursuing a surgical career (15.9% of men, 26.8% of women; P < 0.05). There was no significant difference in when students made the decision to pursue a career in surgery between genders.

Of those pursuing a career in surgery, 54% were women (n ¼ 34) and 44% were men (n ¼ 29). A majority of these students reported verbal discouragement from pursuing a career in surgery (46/61; 75.4%). There was no significant gender difference, with 82% of women and 68% of men reporting discouragement (P ¼ 0.24). This was similar to the overall population of respondents, from which 69% reported discouragement with no significant difference between genders (P ¼ 0.67). Characteristics of Surgery Itself

All participants were asked to rate how characteristics of the career itself influenced their decision to, or not to, pursue a career in surgery (Table 6). Work hours and time for outside interests were reported as a negative concern for the highest number of individuals in groups of both genders, with 85.9% of men and 93.9% of women reporting a negative impact of work hours, and 90.6% of men and 93.4% of women reporting a negative impact of lack of time for outside interests. Significantly more women (75.0%) than men (58.1%) reported that the length of residency negatively impacted their career decision (P ¼ 0.04). There was no significant difference between the genders in terms of impact of work hours, stress levels, medicolegal implications, time for outside interests, personality fit, expected income, competitiveness, and educational debt.

Women were significantly more likely to report concern about time to date or marry (P ¼ 0.04), time available to spend with family (P ¼ 0.02), finding a good time during residency to have a child (P < 0.0001), taking maternity/paternity leave during residency (P < 0.0001), and being too old after residency to have a child (P < 0.0001) (Table 7). Overall 86.2% of women and 83.2% of men in the survey reported that one of the aforementioned reasons dissuaded them or somewhat dissuaded them from pursuing a career in surgery entirely.

Regarding the surgical rotation, both genders expressed positive and negative reflections. Negative comments were largely focused on the time-demand, hierarchy, and culture of surgery. The negative impression of medical student work hours during the surgical rotation compared to other clinical rotations had been described peviously20,21,22 and is a growing concern as more emphasis is placed on the importance of lifestyle and balance in career choice.23 Interestingly, some authors proposed modifying the surgical clerkship to shield the realities of resident work hours and lifestyle,24–27 but misleading trainees under false pretenses could easily translate to dissatisfaction during residency, burnout, and attrition.28 Importantly, the increased prevalence of sharing clinical responsibilities with mid-level providers is likely to decrease the double-burden surgical residents face in managing both the operating room and floor.29 Nonetheless, the time demands of surgery continue to be a deterrent for career choice.

Another key finding was the prevalence of verbal discouragement experienced by all medical students. Nearly 70% of medical students reported being discouraged from pursuing the field, the highest prevalence in the subset of women during the clinical and research/fellowship years. Despite statistically equal discouragement among all subgroups, the women perceived that the verbal remarks were gender-based. Additionally, the cohort of undecided medical students appeared to be most susceptible to familial-related discouragement, as 82.6% of undecided women reported that the majority of verbal discouragement was based on family aspirations. These findings likely associate with our findings on the characteristics of surgery that showed women reporting a significantly higher level of concern about finding a time during residency date or get married, have a child (with the risk of being too old to have children after residency), take maternity or paternity leave, and spend with family in general. The underrepresentation of women in surgical disciplines is related to a multitude of factors, including personal experience, environment, mentorship, and role models. Verbal discouragement of individuals against pursuing a career in surgery is likely to have an impact on all these factors that contribute to medical students lived experience and decision to pursue a career in surgery.

Given that the verbal discouragement and trainees’ concerns are largely based on family aspirations, additional support within the surgical field is needed to mitigate these concerns and support trainees in both their career and familial goals. Family aspirations were also a significant factor for men to choose an alternative career path. Our data corroborate a study by Sanfey et al that demonstrated men and women were equally discouraged from a career in surgery by the opinions of a spouse, family member, or significant other, but a higher percentage of women than men were discouraged by their decision to have a family.26 Importantly, there is an undeniable biological premise in which women are physically the ones to have children, unless surrogacy or adoption is sought, and this becomes more challenging with age. At present, women surgeons delay childbearing and have an increased risk for infertility from both this temporal delay and the stress of their career.30–32 Many women are attempting to mitigate this challenge by planning pregnancy during a research year; however, biology is not always compliant (many women resort to in vitro fertilization and are still unable to become pregnant in that narrow time window) and this is not a sufficient solution.30,31

The challenges that trainees face in achieving their familial goals in concert with their career aspirations predominantly arise from the length of training, its concurrence with female fertility years, and limited flexibility in taking time off to bear a child.33 To expound on this structural problem, a recent study by Rangel et al surveyed surgeons who had 1 pregnancies during an accredited US general surgery residency program.32 Of 347 women surgeons, 297

(85.6%) worked an unmodified schedule until birth, and 220 (63.6%) were concerned that their work schedule adversely affected the health of themselves or their unborn child. After delivery, only 34.9% of residents reported having maternity leave policies. The duration of leave—when given—a majority <6 weeks—was perceived to be inadequate by 72.0% of women, and institutional support for childcare upon return to work was rare. This greatly impacted the morale of women surgeons, as nearly 40% strongly considered leaving residency and one-third said they would discourage female medical students from a surgical career.32 The significant deterrents found in our medical student survey combined with the surgeons’ study by Rangel et al have been reported in other resident populations as well,34 and highlight major issues with the current structure of training and reasons why the sentiment that wanting a family is incongruent with a career in surgery among residents and medical students.

These data and challenges call for systemic change. Clear institutional policies regarding maternity and paternity leave for surgical residents should be established by each hospital or department, and open communication between trainees and faculty regarding family planning should be welcomed. Cultural changes, such as paternity leave and more equitable family roles, would enhance support for female surgeons who have a child during residency or early in their career. In addition, providing more institutional childcare has proven beneficial some residency programs, and should be expanded.35 Finally, mentorship for overcoming the challenges of child bearing and rearing during key career development stages should be expanded.36.

Although this survey provides a recent, cross-sectional examination of medical students’ perceptions of a career in surgery, there are important limitations. As a single-institution study at a private, urban, research institution, these results may not reflect the results at other medical universities. The response rate of 37% limits generalizability; however, the demographic distributions of respondents with respect to interest in surgery, age, and class year were comparable, and stratification of result by gender was done to mitigate bias involving a higher response by women. Additionally, there was no control group in the survey, such as comparing discouragement from surgery to that of internal medicine, which obfuscates understanding of dissuasion in other fields. However, many previous studies have reported on higher rates of gender discrimination in surgical specialties compared to medical specialties, predominantly against women in the all surgical subspecialties, except for obstetrics and gynecology, where more men report gender-based discrimination.37–39 Another study limitation is the absence of data characterizing the individuals responsible for verbal discouragement, which greatly limits the ability to plan interventions. In an upcoming study, we intend to investigate which roles—such as clinical faculty, residents, peer students, and academic advisors—are the greatest influencers and means of encouragement and discouragement for students’ career choice. Inquiring about the influence of nursing and patients may also be worthwhile, as a recent study showed that nurses and patients were the highest perpetrators of gender-based discrimination toward residents.40 The gender of the advice giver could also inform the percent of discouragement by women versus male surgeons. This information is important to understand the boundaries of influence over medical student career choice and help rectify the discouragement students receive and perceived barriers they have against pursuing a career in surgery.

Gastrointestinal bezoars, collections of incompletely digested material within the alimentary tract, can present as a diagnostic challenge and should be considered in the diﬀerential diagnosis and management of small bowel obstruction, ischemic bowel, or bowel perforation. We present a case of a 37-year-old man with a distant history of laparotomy for superior mesenteric artery thrombosis requiring partial small bowel resection of the jejunum who presented with worsening abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and hematemesis. An abdominal computed tomography revealed dilated loops of small bowel with a transition point at the ileum, distal to his prior bowel anastomosis. He was managed initially nonoperatively, but persistent vomiting and worsening distention necessitated urgent exploratory laparotomy. During the procedure, a 4 cm by 3 cm phytobezoar was discovered at the midjejunum. -e patient had an unremarkable postoperative course with no further symptoms at 1-year follow-up. Timely diagnosis and treatment of bezoar is essential to minimize patient complications.

## 1. Introduction

Gastrointestinal bezoars are rare but often can present with serious complications if untreated. While the physical nature of these bezoars varies, the extent to which they can aﬀect the motility of the alimentary tract is also variable, creating a challenge both in diagnosis and management. In this case, we present the clinical, radiographic, and operative ﬁndings of a man who presented with a phytobezoar in the setting of a small bowel obstruction. We also review the existing literature to address the appropriate diagnostic and treatment strategies to minimize perioperative complications.

## 2. Case Presentation

-e patient is a 37-year-old man with a past medical history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, extensive hypercoagulable history, and a remote history of exploratory laparotomy for

an embolectomy of the superior mesenteric artery and a small bowel resection of the jejunum. He presented to the Emergency Department with an 8-hour history of worsening, crampy abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and multiple episodes of hematemesis. He had a bowel movement prior to arrival, but otherwise his review of systems was unremarkable. Physical examination was notable for hemodynamic stability and a mildly distended abdomen with epigastric tenderness but without guarding or rebound tenderness. Given his prior surgical history, a computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen was obtained, which showed dilated loops of bowel with a transition point in the region of the proximal ileum, just distal to his prior bowel anastomosis. -e distended proximal small bowel loops contained fecalized material, and the distal small bowel loops were also decompressed without evidence of ascites, bowel wall enhancement, or free air (Figure 1).

-e patient was admitted and initially managed nonoperatively with ﬂuid resuscitation, pain control, bowel rest with nasogastric tube decompression, and serial abdominal exams. Following return of bowel function, the nasogastric tube was discontinued on hospital day 2 but reinserted hours later due to persistent, new-onset vomiting, and worsening abdominal distention. Without signiﬁcant improvement in symptoms, the patient was taken to the operating room urgently for an exploratory laparotomy. Intraoperatively, the small bowel was dilated to approximately the midjejunum, where an intraluminal obstruction was palpated and subsequently identiﬁed to be a phytobezoar. Consequently, a longitudinal enterotomy was performed to evacuate the phytobezoar measuring 4 cm by 3 cm and was closed in a transverse fashion in two layers (Figure 2). -e phytobezoar seemed to be composed of ﬁbers, but material resembling skins and seeds were not identiﬁed. -ere was also no evidence that this obstruction was located at the suture line, and no other intraluminal pathology was noted that would have narrowed the lumen

of the bowel. Final pathology revealed “vegetable matter and acellular debris.” On further questioning the patient, the patient endorsed a diet prior to hospitalization that was signiﬁcant for large amounts of vegetables. However, because no ﬁner detail was elicited, further conclusions about the content could not be drawn. -e patient continued to progress well postoperatively with eventual return of bowel function and was discharged home without complications. -e patient demonstrated good recovery from his surgery and was asymptomatic at his postoperative clinic visit and at 1-year follow-up.

## 3. Discussion

Gastrointestinal bezoars are collections of incompletely digested material within the alimentary tract that can lead to serious medical complications including small bowel obstruction, bowel ischemia, or perforation. Bezoars are classiﬁed by their contents: phytobezoars involve ﬁbrous nondigestible matter from fruit, vegetables, psyllium, or persimmon (diospyrobezoar); trichobezoars comprised ingested hair, prevalent in women aged less than 30 years; pharmacobezoars arise from enteric-coated aspirin, extended release capsules (nifedipine and theophylline), or sucralfate; and occasionally, bezoars result from ingested styrofoam, fungi, cement, or other inedible objects. While phytobezoars are the most common types of bezoar, phytobezoar-induced small bowel obstruction is a rare clinical situation, accounting for less than 5% of all mechanical intestinal obstructions [1]. Patients with a history of peptic ulcer disease, previous gastric surgeries or bowel resections, and systemic diseases that reduce gastrointestinal motility or cause strictures (e.g., Crohn’s disease, carcinoma of the gastrointestinal tract, chronic dehydration, hypothyroidism, diabetes, and in some cases, connective tissue-related disorders) are predisposed to bezoar formation [2]. Excessive vegetable ﬁber ingestion or alterations in dentition and mastication can also increase one’s risk for complications as the ability to distinguish nutritionally valuable material from that which is not is compromised. Consequently, phytobezoar should be considered as part of the diﬀerential diagnosis for patients with a clinical history, similar to our patient, who presented with symptoms of bowel obstruction or an acute surgical abdomen, especially when no obvious underlining mechanical or physiological causes of obstruction can be identiﬁed. Likewise, the presence of bezoars should be considered in patients with an extensive psychiatric history who present with bowel obstruction, although most often, this aspect is ignored during initial patient evaluation, given its relative rarity. Lastly, patients with gastroparesis may also be susceptible to gastric outlet syndrome if they develop a phytobezoar [3]. In patients with small bowel obstruction due to phytobezoar, the ileum is the most common site of obstruction [4]. Two recent case reports also emphasize this ﬁnding. In the ﬁrst case, a 55-year-old male with a previous gastrectomy presented with an ileal phytobezoar causing small bowel obstruction. -e second case involved a patient from Iran

While our patient had no dietary history persimmons consumption, he endorsed a recent diet signiﬁcant for large amounts of vegetables. Further information on the speciﬁcs of his diet was lacking, but we suspect that consumption of large amounts of vegetables rich in ﬁber (e.g., ﬁgs, sauerkraut, brussels sprouts, and potato peel), which are composed of cellulose, hemicellulose, or tannins, could have been the source of the phytobezoar. Radiographically, phytobezoars are well-circumscribed intraluminal masses that have a heterogeneous appearance, often with a mottled, air-bubble pattern and an absence of mesenteric fat stranding [6]. -ey can be seen with abdominal radiography, ultrasonography, or CT as a mass or a ﬁlling defect. A recent study of bezoars in China by Kuang et al. examined risk factors for small bowel obstruction caused by bezoars and found that major diameter measured on CTscans was a signiﬁcant independent predictor [7]. In general, bezoars most commonly occur in the distal small intestine or the jejunum and in some cases, are associated with Meckel’s diverticula in the ileum [7]. -e radiographic appearance of the bezoar on CT scan may be similar to the fecalized small bowel content seen with established small bowel obstructions (Figure 2). Furthermore, there are no reports of phytobezoar-induced ileus, to our knowledge, that was diagnosed preoperatively. -us, preoperative diagnosis of phytobezoar is unlikely as opposed to small bowel obstruction. In our patient, deﬁnite diagnosis of phytobezoar prior to surgical removal was not possible and perhaps also not possible retrospectively given the nonspeciﬁc appearance of fecalized small bowel content and the limited ability of CTscans to distinguish ﬁner details of the mass. Notably, our patient had no obvious areas of intrinsic bowel stenosis, and this location of the bezoar was more distal than the prior bowel anastomosis and more proximal than the natural narrowing at the level of a Meckel’s diverticulum. -e rare midjejunal location of the obstruction in our patient likely was a combination of intra-abdominal adhesions and the continual accretions of the phytobezoar. Diagnosis of bezoar is often delayed, but once established, there are several treatment options available. Medically, treatment with prokinetic agents such as itopride, mosapride, and metoclopramide or enzymatic breakdown (dissolution) is often suﬃcient. If the lesion is conﬁned to the stomach or duodenum, endoscopic fragmentation with forceps or snares can be employed to diagnose and deconstruct the bezoar with a goal of alleviating the bowel obstruction. Additionally, for gastric bezoars, Coca-Cola has been shown to be an eﬀective dissolution agent [8]. For those with failure to progress or worsening clinical symptoms, surgery is the gold standard method to avoid bowel ischemia and bezoar-induced pressure necrosis. -is almost always involves an exploratory laparoscopy or laparotomy with bowel enterotomies with or without primary resection. Intraoperatively, the bezoar may be fragmented and “milked” to the cecum or resected via enterotomy.

Timely diagnosis and treatment of bezoar is essential to minimize patient complications, although in most scenarios, this task is diﬃcult to accomplish. In the current era, the utility and dependence of imaging to aid in the diagnosis cannot be underestimated. -erefore, bezoar obstruction, although rare, should be an important consideration, especially during the initial evaluation and workup of patients presenting with abdominal symptoms to the emergency room.
